overview: Germany reunited on 3 October 1990 when the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic. The 1949 Basic Law’s promise to protect human dignity continued, but unification involved real changes to jobs, schools, medicine and daily routines. People from the former East and West did not all have the same experiences. Earlier worker migration and later family histories also made Germany multilingual. The imported map begins in 1994, four years after the political event. Germany continues as a federal republic.

periods.title: Reunification before this map
periods.summary: The GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The imported 1994 start is later and does not mark the legal beginning of unity.

periods.title: Institutions and households adjust
periods.summary: Eastern schools and health systems changed under the national legal framework; families navigated jobs, homes and services.

periods.title: Continuing federal republic
periods.summary: Germany continues with constitutional protections, different regional experiences and multilingual family histories.

items.text: On 3 October 1990, East Germany joined the Federal Republic under the Unification Treaty. The map’s 1994 start is four years later, so the card follows the legal date, not the first available polygon.

East Germans held a free parliamentary election in March 1990 after peaceful protests and the Berlin Wall’s opening. Their choices mattered in how unity happened; it was more than politicians redrawing a border.

The Basic Law begins, “Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar,” meaning “Human dignity is inviolable.” This short written German line became a constitutional guide for the reunited country. It is a promise the state must keep working to honor.

Reunification did not erase differences in wages, public services or family memories. The Federal Archives describes the difficult state of some eastern health facilities around 1989-94 and emergency support that kept care going.

The unification treaty recognized school and professional qualifications earned in the GDR. Imagine finishing school just as the state on your diploma disappears: the rule helped graduates continue their studies or work. State education systems still had to adapt.

Before 1990, West Germany recruited workers from Italy, Turkey, Spain and other countries. Some stayed, reunited with family and raised children in Germany. Reunification inherited this history; German family life never had only one language or one origin.

The 2022 German housing census still records a home’s WC and bath as separate features. That may sound fussy until you ask whether a family has a private place to wash as well as a toilet. Housing quality remains a real-life question beneath an orderly country outline.

A household might carry memories of a crowded postwar room, a GDR prefab apartment or a West German worker dormitory into the same reunited country. These are different family stories, and no one example should stand for all Germans.

Germany remains a federal republic. The former GDR ended as a separate state in 1990 when it joined the Federal Republic; people from both sides continued. The 1878-1945 “Germany” record is a separate map-era label, not today’s founding date.

The Basic Law, schools, and civic life continue to change. Remembering the Holocaust and the divided years helps explain why human dignity, democratic choice and family stories are central to this card.

ending.text: Germany continues as a federal republic after the GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The imported 1994 map start is later than reunification. East and West Germans, migrant families and other communities carried different histories into the continuing state.
